chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazee' from his uncle Hamzah ibn Bazee' from Ali ibn Suwayd from Al-Rida (peace be upon him) regarding what we know.

He said: 'In the funeral prayer, you recite Al-Fatihah in the first standing, send blessings upon the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) in the second, supplicate for the believing men and women in the third, supplicate for your deceased in the fourth, and the fifth is for turning away (concluding).'

The beginning of this report is that he said from Al-Rida (peace be upon him) 'regarding what we know', and he did not narrate it with certainty, but rather narrated it with doubt. And when the narrator is doubtful about the one he reports from, it is permissible that he erred in his statement 'you recite in the first [standing] with Al-Fatihah'.

And also, he narrated - 441-13 - Ahmad ibn Muhammad from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Muhammad ibn Isma'il ibn Bazee' from his uncle from Ali ibn Suwayd al-Sa'i from Abu al-Hasan al-Awwal (peace be upon him): 'Like that.'

And in this narration he reported from Abu al-Hasan al-Awwal, meaning Musa (peace be upon him), and in the first narration from Al-Rida (peace be upon him), while the narrator is one person. And this indicates that he erred in the original report.

And if it were sound, it would be attributed to a type of precautionary piety (taqiyyah), because it agrees with the opinions of some of the Sunnis. And that which indicates that there is no recitation in the funeral prayer is what he narrated:

key_terms.بِأُمِّ الْكِتَابِ: With the Mother of the Book (Al-Fatihah)

ai.seo_question: Is recitation of Al-Fatihah required in the first standing of the funeral prayer according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Tusi's *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights a scholarly debate regarding the necessity of reciting Al-Fatihah in the first standing of the funeral prayer, citing Imam al-Rida (AS) with a degree of uncertainty. The scholar suggests the report may reflect *taqiyyah* or be an error, aligning with the dominant Shia view that no recitation is required, thereby contrasting with Sunni practices. This discussion underscores the methodological rigor in evaluating chain reliability and the theological implications of ritual uniformity.
